paragraphs.source_en:
(‘Alas, when in the garden wither the mallows, the green celery, and the luxuriant curled
anise, they live again thereafter and spring up another year, but we men, we that are tall and
strong, we that are wise, when once we die, unhearing sleep in the hollow earth, a long sleep
without end or wakening.’)
 The premature and arrested spring of stanza xvi is now supplanted by the emergence of true
spring.
 Recalling the archetypal classical statement of this sentiment in the Pervigilium Veneris ll.

paragraphs.source_en:
(‘The Spring, the new, the warb’ling Spring appears,
The youthful Season of reviving Years;
In Spring the Loves enkindle mutual Heats,
The feather’d Nation chuse their tuneful Mates,
The Trees grow fruitful with descending Rain
And drest in diff ’ring Greens adorn the Plain.’
 Trans. Thomas Parnell (1722))
155. the revolving year] Cp. l. 472. ‘Revolving’ is used in the sense of ‘mov[ing] round its regular
course’ (OED 3).
 Cp. Song of Solomon ii 11–13: ‘For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; The flowers
appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our
land’.
